_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run cases (npm run check:golden plant-rescue). Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200, no truncation. V2 REWRITE (2026-09-06): replaced a forced diagnosis (single primary_problem, numeric identification confidence_score, is_saveable boolean, a recovery_timeline, a 12-month seasonal calendar, an unconditional propagation_guide with a success_rate) with an evidence-first structure grounded only in what was reported/visible. One endpoint (/api/plant-rescue) now dispatches on mode (rescue|care|identify) to three distinct schemas instead of the old parallel-split diagnose+care calls — the new schemas are lean enough (no calendar, no forced repotting/propagation) that a single call per mode is fast without needing the split. Rescue: plant_identification{best_match,scientific_name,confidence,why_it_fits,alternatives,what_would_confirm} / bottom_line{attention_level,summary} / what_you_reported[] / possible_explanations[]{possibility,why_it_could_fit,check} / check_first[]{check,what_to_look_for,if_yes,if_no} / what_to_do_now[]{action,why,condition} / what_improvement_looks_like[] / safety{show,who_or_what,guidance} / useful_next_photo. Care: plant{name,scientific_name,confidence} / core_care{light,watering,soil_and_drainage,feeding,temperature_and_humidity} / repot_when[] / when_conditions_change[]{condition,adjustment} / watch_for[] / pet_child_safety{show,guidance}. Identify: best_match{common_name,scientific_name,confidence,why_it_fits[]} / alternatives[]{name,why_possible,how_to_distinguish} / what_would_help_confirm[] / safety_note{show,guidance}. attention_level is one of likely_minor|watch_and_check|needs_attention|serious_damage_possible — never a percentage, never saveable/not-saveable. confidence is high|moderate|low — never a numeric percentage. router.outputStandard='v2' + router.outputGuard with runOutputGuard (LLM-judge check + repair) — same mechanism as Pet Behavior Decoder, since the failure mode here is invented facts (a cause, a schedule, a recovery timeline), not fixed-vocabulary phrasing. Follow-up now passes forward REPORTED/POSSIBILITIES/CHECKS structured context instead of a flattened 'Diagnosis: [claim]' string, and is explicitly allowed to revise the earlier interpretation. Companion planting reframed from an 'indoor plant placement expert' inventing rooms/windows/air-purifying claims to CARE COMPATIBILITY grouping only (good_to_group/better_kept_apart/placement_principle), no automatic upsell to buy more plants. Input form changes: 'What do you see?' -> 'What's happening?'; 'Bad smell/possible root rot' symptom relabeled to plain 'Bad smell' (no pre-supposed diagnosis in a checkbox label); the old ageOfOwnership free-text field replaced by a symptomDuration dropdown (owner reports ownership duration, if relevant, in free text instead — the PLANT AGE/OWNERSHIP prompt rule explicitly warns against converting either into horticultural history); new 'Has anything changed recently?' checklist; old flat wateringFreq bucket (daily/few-days/weekly/rarely) replaced by a wateringMethod practice question (checks soil first / fixed schedule / waits for thirsty signs / varies) plus an optional free-text frequency, since a calendar interval alone can't establish over- or under-watering; new optional hasDrainage yes/no/not-sure. A client-side detectFieldConflict()-style check was NOT added here (unlike Pet Behavior Decoder) since no equivalent hard numeric contradiction exists in this input set — the model's own INPUT CONFLICTS rule handles the softer cases (a symptom selection vs. free text) that can arise. IDENTIFY MODE PROVENANCE fix (2026-09-06, same day): identification evidence must come only from the CURRENT photo — Rescue-mode symptoms, Care-mode information, watering/light/move history, a previous plant description, saved-plant history, and a previous analysis's conclusion must never be used as evidence for botanical identity, only retained as context, with any conflict between the current photo and prior context surfaced rather than blended. Fixed at two layers: (1) the frontend now sends ONLY imageBase64 + mode + plantName for an Identify-mode request — Rescue/Care fields left in state from switching tabs without resetting are no longer sent at all, closing the realistic leak path; (2) a new IDENTIFY MODE PROVENANCE prompt rule + outputGuard.prohibit category is the defense-in-depth backstop for any request that reaches the backend with that context anyway (verified directly against the API, bypassing the frontend fix, in the new 'identify-does-not-use-prior-plant-history-as-visual-evidence' case below). MODE STATE ISOLATION + CARE REDESIGN (2026-09-06, same day, later pass): manually switching mode tabs now clears every prior mode's form fields and result via handleReset() (My Plants and saved history are exempt); two explicit handoffs build on the same reset — handleShowCareFromIdentify (Identify result -> Care, carries the photo + seeds careSpecies) and handleCheckAgain (My Plants -> Rescue, carries only that plant's identity). Care mode's inputs were redesigned around normal growing conditions instead of symptoms: new careSpecies/careWhereIsIt/careLight (6-option, its own scale)/careHelpWith fields, deliberately kept separate from Rescue's lightLevel/location rather than merged; Care no longer shows symptom checkboxes, duration, or recent-changes. The 'care-pothos-thriving' case's input was updated to the new field names to match. A separate bug found while live-testing this (not caused by it): Identify mode could falsely claim no photo was supplied when one was — see the new 'identify-does-not-falsely-claim-no-photo-was-provided' case for the fix and its documented non-deterministic residual. THREE MORE FIXES (2026-09-06, same day, third pass, found live-testing the above): (1) the backend's shared non-identify validation still checked plantDescription/symptoms (Rescue's fields) for Care too, so a valid careSpecies-only submission — Care has no symptom checkboxes — was rejected with Rescue-flavored 400 copy; Care now has its own branch requiring careSpecies or a photo, matching the intended design where a common name is enough and the model supplies the rest (see 'care-species-name-only-no-other-fields'). (2) The 'Try an example' header pill hardcoded near-black text and a black/25 border, invisible against this tool's deliberately-dark headerColor (see src/utils/headerGradient.js) once blended with a dark page background; text/border now flip with isDark, alpha stays the standard '80' so the PF-17b header-pill audit pattern still matches. (3) Opening 'My Plants' and saving a plant both used revealSection's default block:'start', slamming the panel to the very top of the viewport — a much bigger jump than necessary for a short, in-place disclosure panel (unlike a full results screen); both now use block:'nearest'. handleSavePlant also now opens the collection and moves focus to it directly, not only via the showCollection effect, so it fires whether or not the panel was already open. FOURTH PASS (2026-09-06, same day): IDENTIFY IMAGE CONSISTENCY — the Identify schema was restructured from four independent top-level fields (best_match, alternatives, what_would_help_confirm, safety_note) to current_image_present (set by CODE from imageBase64, never trusted from the model) plus one identification_evidence object {current_image_observations, best_match{common_name,scientific_name,identity_source}, confidence, distinguishing_visible_features, plausible_alternatives, unresolved_identification_questions} that every section reads from, so no section can independently assume a photo exists while another assumes it doesn't. The false-no-photo-claim guard from the third pass was moved to run LAST, after the v2 guard's own repair step (a repair can rewrite a flagged field without knowing the code's ground truth and reintroduce the exact contradiction it was meant to fix), and its regex broadened to catch a stray interposed word ('No image DATA was received') and a softer denial ('Without a photo, ...') — re-verified 6/6 clean with the regenerate step visibly catching 2 along the way. PLANT IDENTITY PROVENANCE: new identity_source field ('visitor_supplied'|'photo_identified'|'unclear') added to Rescue's plant_identification, Care's plant, and Identify's identification_evidence.best_match — confidence badges are no longer shown for a visitor-supplied identity the tool didn't independently confirm ('Identity supplied by you' displays instead), since confidence describes the tool's own identification, not the visitor's. PRACTICAL PRECISION: new GENERAL_RULES paragraph (applies to all 3 modes, not just Rescue's existing rescue-flavored 'NO ARBITRARY PRECISION') bans numeric thresholds that don't change the advice if altered — 'push a chopstick 5-7cm' becomes 'check below the dry surface layer with a finger or wooden chopstick,' 'four to six hours of direct light' becomes a plain description of the light category. Existing golden references containing this pattern (care-pothos-thriving's light field, care-species-name-only's watering field, and the rescue case's soil-check depth) were corrected to match. CARE SCHEDULE RENAMED: '💧 Care Schedule' -> '🌿 Your Care Guide' (13 languages) since it was never a schedule; the plain-text copy output's matching emoji was updated too for consistency. COMPANION CHECK REWORDED: good_to_group/better_kept_apart (two buckets, and 'apart' implied physical separation) replaced with a single pairs[] array carrying a three-way verdict (good_match|separate_care|different_needs) and 'why' text that describes what a shared ROUTINE gets wrong rather than suggesting the plants can't be near each other — see the two companions cases below, the second using the exact Jade Plant + Pothos worked example from feedback.

input.plantDescription: Pothos in a 6-inch pot. Leaves yellowing from the bottom up over the past two weeks. A few have brown tips. New growth still green but smaller than before.

plant_identification.why_it_fits: You identified the plant directly, and no contradictory evidence was supplied.
plant_identification.what_would_confirm: Identity is already supplied by you; no further confirmation needed.

bottom_line.summary: Yellowing from the bottom up with still-green new growth is a recognizable pattern in pothos, and a few explanations fit. The plant is not in crisis — new growth continuing is a meaningful positive sign — but the smaller new leaves suggest something in its conditions deserves a closer look before it progresses further.

what_you_reported: Leaves yellowing from the bottom up over the past two weeks
A few leaves have brown tips
New growth is still green but smaller than before
Waters on a fixed weekly schedule

possible_explanations.why_it_could_fit: A fixed weekly schedule does not account for how quickly the mix actually dries out, which varies with season, temperature, and root mass. If the soil is still wet at watering time, lower leaves — which are older and more vulnerable — tend to yellow first. Brown tips can also accompany waterlogged roots.
possible_explanations.check: Push a finger an inch or two into the potting mix. If it still feels wet or cool rather than barely moist, watering is likely happening before the plant needs it.

possible_explanations.possibility: Natural lower-leaf senescence, possibly accelerated by a care or environment change
possible_explanations.why_it_could_fit: Pothos regularly shed older lower leaves as a normal process, especially if light is limited or conditions recently shifted — a season change, a move, or a change in routine. This pattern looks similar to overwatering, so the two need to be distinguished.
possible_explanations.check: Look at how many leaves are affected and whether yellowing is actively spreading. If only a small number of the oldest, lowest leaves have yellowed and new growth continues, this is more consistent with normal turnover than a problem taking hold.

possible_explanations.possibility: Light on the low end for sustained healthy growth
possible_explanations.why_it_could_fit: Pothos tolerates low light but can show reduced leaf size and gradual lower-leaf loss when light is consistently limited. Smaller new leaves alongside older yellowing leaves could suggest the plant is getting less usable light than it needs to sustain its current size.
possible_explanations.check: Note whether the new growth is reaching or leaning toward the light source, and how far the plant sits from the nearest window. If it is more than a few feet from a window or the window faces away from the sun, light may be a contributing factor.

check_first.what_to_look_for: Is the potting mix still damp an inch or two down when you water each week?
check_first.if_yes: Hold off watering and let the mix dry further before the next watering. Shift from a fixed schedule to checking the soil each time.
check_first.if_no: Watering frequency is likely fine. Focus attention on light and whether the yellowing is spreading.

check_first.what_to_look_for: Count roughly how many leaves are affected and whether new ones are yellowing now or the problem seems contained to a few old lower leaves.
check_first.if_yes: If it is spreading to newer leaves, that points away from normal senescence and toward a care issue worth correcting.
check_first.if_no: If only the oldest leaves at the base are affected and it seems to have slowed, normal leaf turnover is plausible.

check_first.what_to_look_for: How far is the plant from the window, and is the new growth noticeably smaller than growth you have seen before in this spot?
check_first.if_yes: If the plant is far from the window or in a corner, moving it closer to a bright indirect light source is worth trying.
check_first.if_no: If position has not changed and growth was normal before the past two weeks, light is less likely to be the primary trigger.

what_to_do_now.action: Switch from a fixed watering schedule to checking soil moisture before each watering
what_to_do_now.why: A weekly interval may be landing before the mix has dried enough, which is the most common driver of this symptom pattern in pothos. Watering only when the top inch or two of mix has dried out removes the guesswork.
what_to_do_now.condition: Do this regardless of which explanation turns out to be correct — it is a safe adjustment and rules out the most actionable cause.

what_to_do_now.action: Remove fully yellowed leaves cleanly at the stem
what_to_do_now.why: They will not recover, and removing them keeps you from mistaking old damage for new spreading.
what_to_do_now.condition: Only leaves that are fully yellow — leave any that still have green, as they may stabilize.

what_to_do_now.action: Move closer to a brighter indirect light source if the plant is currently far from a window
what_to_do_now.why: Smaller new leaves alongside lower-leaf yellowing can indicate the plant is working with less light than it would prefer. A modest improvement in light position is low-risk for a pothos.
what_to_do_now.condition: Only if the check suggests light is limited — avoid direct harsh sun, which can scorch pothos leaves.

what_improvement_looks_like: Yellowing stops spreading to newer leaves
New leaves emerge at a similar or larger size than previous growth
No new brown tips appearing on healthy green leaves
Soil is drying to the expected depth between waterings, confirming the new schedule is calibrated

safety.guidance: Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) is considered toxic to cats and dogs if ingested, primarily due to insoluble calcium oxalates. If a pet chews or eats any part of the plant, contact your vet or an animal poison-information service. Keep the plant out of reach as a precaution.

output.useful_next_photo: A close photo of one of the yellowing leaves — showing whether the yellowing is uniform across the leaf or patterned (veins staying green, edges affected first, etc.) — would help narrow the cause if the soil-moisture check does not resolve things.

input.plantDescription: Healthy pothos, want to know how to keep it thriving.

core_care.light: Pothos tolerates a wide range, and bright indirect light keeps growth vigorous and variegation vivid. It will survive lower light but may grow more slowly and lose color contrast — compare growth rate and leaf color to a spot with more usable light if you're not sure it's getting enough.
core_care.watering: You are already doing the right thing by checking the soil first. Pothos tolerates partial light well and does not need frequent watering — most problems come from too much water rather than too little. The drainage and your habit of checking before watering is what keeps it thriving. Watch for changes: if the plant moves to darker conditions, soil stays wet longer and you will water less often. If it moves closer to light, the soil will dry faster and you may need to check more frequently.
core_care.soil_and_drainage: A well-draining all-purpose potting mix works well. The drainage hole you have is important — keep it clear.
core_care.feeding: Pothos does not require feeding to stay healthy. If you notice new growth slowing or leaves losing color over several weeks, that is the time to consider whether the soil needs nutrient replenishment. Most pothos in indoor homes stay thriving without supplemental feeding for years.
core_care.temperature_and_humidity: Pothos does well in typical indoor temperate conditions. Keep it away from cold drafts, air conditioning vents, and heating sources. It tolerates average household humidity without any special intervention.

repot_when: Roots are circling the bottom of the pot or pushing out of the drainage hole and growth has noticeably stalled.
The potting mix dries out extremely fast — within a day of watering — because roots have displaced most of the soil.
The plant is visibly top-heavy or unstable in its current pot.

when_conditions_change.condition: Light drops — shorter days, moved to a darker spot, or window blocked seasonally
when_conditions_change.adjustment: Soil will dry more slowly. Check moisture before watering rather than keeping any set interval, and expect to water less often.

when_conditions_change.condition: The plant is near a heat source in winter or in a warm dry room
when_conditions_change.adjustment: Soil may dry faster than usual — check it more frequently.

when_conditions_change.condition: You notice a burst of new growth
when_conditions_change.adjustment: Water demand may increase slightly. Keep checking the soil rather than adjusting to a fixed schedule.

watch_for: Yellow leaves — can signal overwatering if soil stays wet for extended periods, or occasionally underwatering if the plant has been very dry.
Brown, crispy leaf tips — often a sign of dry air, inconsistent watering, or the plant sitting in a draft.
Leggy, stretched stems with wide gaps between leaves — usually means it wants more light.
Wilting that does not recover after watering — worth checking that the drainage hole is not blocked.
Small dark or mushy patches on stems near the soil — inspect the base and reduce watering if found.

pet_child_safety.guidance: Pothos is toxic to humans if ingested, including children. The plant contains calcium oxalate crystals, which can cause mouth irritation, swelling, and stomach upset. Keep it out of reach of young children who might chew on leaves or stems. If ingestion occurs, contact Poison Control (in the US: 1-800-222-1222) for guidance.

cases.name: care-species-name-only-no-other-fields
cases.why_this_case_exists: Permanent regression guard (2026-09-06) for a bug found live-testing: the backend's non-identify validation still checked plantDescription/symptoms — Rescue's fields — so a complete, valid Care submission carrying only careSpecies (Care has no symptom checkboxes and description is optional context) was rejected with the 400 'Provide a photo, description, or select symptoms.' error, Rescue-flavored copy that doesn't even apply to Care's form. Fixed by giving Care its own branch: careSpecies (trimmed) or a photo satisfies it. This is also the intended design — a common name is enough input; the model supplies the rest.

core_care.light: Pothos tolerates a wide range of light, adapting from bright indirect light to lower-light corners, though it grows fastest and keeps the strongest color in brighter indirect light.
core_care.watering: Check below the dry surface layer with a finger or wooden chopstick — water once it no longer feels moist there, rather than on a fixed schedule.
core_care.soil_and_drainage: A well-draining all-purpose potting mix in a pot with drainage holes is what matters most.
core_care.feeding: A balanced liquid fertilizer during active growth is optional; hold off if growth has slowed.
core_care.temperature_and_humidity: Typical indoor temperatures and average household humidity suit pothos without special treatment.

repot_when: Roots are visibly circling the inside of the pot or pushing densely out of drainage holes.
Water runs straight through without being absorbed.
The plant tips over easily because it has become root-heavy for its pot.

when_conditions_change.adjustment: Soil dries more slowly — check moisture before watering rather than keeping the same interval.

watch_for: Yellow leaves — check whether the soil is staying wet.
Brown, mushy stems at the base — a sign of rot from prolonged wet soil.

pet_child_safety.guidance: Pothos is toxic to dogs and cats — contact a vet or pet poison helpline if ingested.

cases.name: identify-no-plant-visible
cases.why_this_case_exists: A solid-color image with no visible plant features must not produce a hallucinated identification — this is the permanent regression guard against inventing a plant identity from an unusable photo.

current_image_observations: The image is a solid green rectangle with no visible plant features — no leaves, stems, texture, or form are present to analyze.
unresolved_identification_questions: A photo showing the actual plant — ideally including leaves, stems, and overall shape
A close-up of the leaf surface and edges if the plant is small or the detail is subtle
Any visible flowers, fruit, or soil context would also help

cases.name: identify-does-not-use-prior-plant-history-as-visual-evidence
cases.why_this_case_exists: Permanent regression guard for the IDENTIFY MODE PROVENANCE rule (2026-09-06). A saved plant's history (from an earlier Rescue check on a DIFFERENT plant, in this fixture) must never be used as evidence for identifying the CURRENT photo — only what's actually visible counts. Sent directly against the API (bypassing the frontend, which as of this fix no longer sends priorObservations/plantDescription/symptoms on an Identify-mode request at all) to verify the backend prompt rule holds as its own defense-in-depth layer, not just the frontend gating.

priorObservations.reported: Fiddle leaf fig, dropped six leaves after being moved near a draftier window.
priorObservations.suggestedChecks: Check soil moisture and light exposure

current_image_observations: The image does not contain enough detail to identify the plant or assess its condition. A clear, close photo showing leaves, stems, and any visible damage or discoloration would let you compare what you are seeing to specific problems.
unresolved_identification_questions: A clear photo of the actual plant, showing leaves, stems, and overall shape.
A close-up of the leaf surface and edges if leaf detail is available.
A photo of the whole plant in its pot or growing location.

cases.name: identify-does-not-falsely-claim-no-photo-was-provided
cases.why_this_case_exists: Permanent regression guard (2026-09-06) for a bug found while live-testing the mode-isolation/Care redesign: given an ambiguous, non-photographic test image (a solid-color placeholder here, standing in for the flat cartoon-illustration test case that surfaced it), the model would sometimes claim outright that no photo/image was supplied, even though one plainly was — reproduced via direct API calls that bypassed the frontend, and confirmed byte-for-byte against a raw out-of-band SDK call that the transport was never the problem. A correct response may say the image is unclear, low-detail, or doesn't show a plant — it must never claim no image exists. Strengthened same day (IDENTIFY IMAGE CONSISTENCY pass): current_image_present is now set by CODE from imageBase64, never trusted from the model, and every section (identification, confidence, observations, alternatives, safety) reads from one identification_evidence object instead of deciding independently whether a photo exists. A reject-and-regenerate check runs as the LAST step, after the v2 guard's own repair pass (a repair can rewrite a flagged field's text without knowing the code's ground truth about the photo, so it can reintroduce this exact contradiction as easily as fix it — checking only the original generation missed that). Re-tested 6/6 clean in the final verified batch, with the regenerate step visibly firing and correcting 2 of those before the response reached the client — a real improvement over the original ~5/6, though still not a mathematical guarantee against a sufficiently novel denial phrasing the regex misses.

current_image_observations: The image doesn't contain enough visible detail to identify a specific plant — no distinguishable leaves, stems, or form are present to work from.
unresolved_identification_questions: A clearer photo of the actual plant, showing leaves, stems, and overall shape.
A close-up of the leaf surface and edges if leaf detail is available.

cases.name: companions-pothos-and-cactus-different-needs
cases.why_this_case_exists: Renamed and restructured (2026-09-06) after feedback that 'better_kept_apart' reads as if the plants shouldn't be physically near each other, when the verdict is actually about care routines. Replaced the two-bucket good_to_group/better_kept_apart shape with one pairs[] array carrying a three-way verdict (good_match|separate_care|different_needs), and reworded 'why' to describe what a shared ROUTINE gets wrong rather than suggesting separation. The Jade Plant + Pothos worked example from feedback is exercised directly in a second case below.

pairs.why: Pothos wants bright indirect light and weekly watering, while the cactus needs full sun and very infrequent watering — these two need genuinely separate routines, not a shared spot or schedule.

output.placement_principle: Put the cactus in your sunniest spot (a south- or west-facing window with direct sun) and the pothos somewhere with bright but filtered light, watering each on its own schedule.

cases.name: companions-jade-and-pothos-different-needs-not-keep-apart
cases.why_this_case_exists: The exact worked example from feedback: a Jade Plant (bright direct sun, fully dry between waterings) and a Pothos (indirect/low light, consistent moisture) should be verdict different_needs with wording like 'these two routines should run independently' — never framed as the plants needing to be kept apart physically.

plants.name: Jade Plant
plants.lightNeeds: Bright direct sun, tolerates full sun
plants.waterNeeds: Let soil dry out completely between waterings, drought-tolerant succulent

plants.name: Pothos
plants.waterNeeds: Prefers consistent moisture, water when top inch is dry

pairs.why: Jade wants bright direct sun and fully dry soil between waterings; Pothos prefers indirect or low light and consistent moisture. The same placement and watering schedule would either sunburn the Pothos or rot it from overwatering, or leave the Jade too dim and too wet.

output.placement_principle: Give the Jade Plant your sunniest spot and water only when the soil is completely dry; find the Pothos a lower-light location and check it when the top inch of soil feels dry — these two routines should run independently.

cases.name: followup-repot-just-in-case
cases.why_this_case_exists: A follow-up asking to repot 'just in case' must not agree merely because it sounds cautious — CHECK BEFORE YOU TREAT and REPOTTING both say not to repot without evidence it would help.

input.question: Should I repot it now just in case?

check_first.check: Check soil moisture before next watering

output.answer:
Repotting isn't something I'd do just in case — it adds stress to the plant and doesn't address the most likely issue here. The original concern was whether the soil is staying too wet between waterings, and repotting doesn't answer that question.

Before anything else, check the soil moisture now: push a finger about two inches in, or lift the pot to feel its weight. If the soil feels wet or heavy, that's meaningful. If it's dry, that points somewhere else.

Repotting would make sense if you find the roots are circling the pot heavily or pushing out of the drainage holes — that's a reason to consider it. But without checking first, you'd be solving a problem you haven't confirmed exists yet.
